**EF4 Tornado**

**[Catoosa County](https://www.weather.gov/ffc/2011_tornadoes_5_year_anniv)**

A National Weather Service survey team determined that an EF4 tornado with winds of 175 MPH occurred in Catoosa County. It touched down approximately 815 PM EDT Wednesday evening along Davis Ridge Road, traveling through Ringgold to Cohutta and into Tennessee. The path length was 13 miles with a width of one third of a mile. Seven fatalities and 30 injuries occurred with this tornado. 75 to 100 homes were damaged or destroyed. The worst damage was located on Cherokee Valley Road where 12 homes were obliterated.

[![Image 1: [ Path of EF-4 tornado that struck Catoosa county. ]](https://www.weather.gov/images/ffc/events/20110427/RinggoldEF4TornadoPath_sm.jpg)](https://www.weather.gov/images/ffc/events/20110427/RinggoldEF4TornadoPath.jpg)

 Path of EF-4 tornado that struck Catoosa County

**EF3 Tornadoes**

**[Dade and Walker Counties](https://www.weather.gov/ffc/2011_tornadoes_5_year_anniv)**

A National Weather Service survey team determined that an EF3 tornado with winds of 150 MPH occurred in Dade and Walker Counties. The tornado moved across the state line into Dade County around 5 miles southwest of Trenton at approximately 535 PM EDT, and lifted just west of Fort Oglethorpe in Walker County around 557 PM EDT. The path length was 18 miles with a width of six tenths of a mile. Note that this path length ONLY includes the area in Georgia (the tornado tracked into Georgia from Alabama). Homes were destroyed, 18 with major damage and tens of thousands of trees were downed. There were 2 fatalities and 12 injuries with this storm.

[![Image 2: [ Path of EF-3 tornado that struck Dade and Walker Counties ]](https://www.weather.gov/images/ffc/events/20110427/TrentonEF3TornadoPath_sm.jpg)](https://www.weather.gov/images/ffc/events/20110427/TrentonEF3TornadoPath.jpg)

 Path of EF-3 tornado that struck Dade and Walker Counties

**[Bartow, Cherokee, and Pickens Counties](https://www.weather.gov/ffc/2011_tornadoes_5_year_anniv)**

A National Weather Service survey team along with the Cherokee county Emergency Management determined that an EF3 tornado with winds of 150 MPH touched down around 925 PM EDT Wednesday evening. It tracked from 5 miles northeast of Kingston in Bartow County, crossing northwest Cherokee County, and lifted approximately 7 miles west of Jasper in Pickens County near the intersection of Jerusalem Church Road and State Highway 53 at approximately 945 PM EDT. The path length was 23 miles and width was a half mile. Several chicken houses were destroyed along Interstate 75, several outbuildings were destroyed and hundreds of trees were downed in Bartow County. Hundreds of trees were snapped or uprooted in Cherokee County. Extensive damage was reported along Henderson Mountain Road and Bryant Road in Pickens County where several mobile homes were destroyed. At least 3 injuries were reported with this tornado, two in Bartow and one in Pickens.

[![Image 3: [ Path of EF-3 tornado that struck Bartow, Cherokee, and Pickens Counties ]](https://www.weather.gov/images/ffc/events/20110427/bartow_cherokee_pickens_tor_track_2011april27_sm.png)](https://www.weather.gov/images/ffc/events/20110427/bartow_cherokee_pickens_tor_track_2011april27.png)

 Path of EF-3 tornado that struck Bartow, Cherokee, and Pickens Counties

**[Meriwether, Spalding, and Henry Counties](https://www.weather.gov/ffc/2011_tornadoes_5_year_anniv)**

A National Weather Service survey team determined that an EF3 tornado with winds of 140 MPH touched down 6 miles north northeast of Gay in Meriwether County at approximately 1203 AM EDT Thursday morning. It tracked across Spalding county and lifted 2 miles south of Hampton in Henry county at approximately 1228 AM EDT. The tornado had a path length of 20 miles and a width of half of a mile.

[![Image 4: [ Path of EF-3 tornado that struck Meriwether, Spalding, and Henry counties ]](https://www.weather.gov/images/ffc/events/20110427/spalding_tor_track_2011april27_sm.png)](https://www.weather.gov/images/ffc/events/20110427/spalding_tor_track_2011april27.png)

 Path of EF-3 tornado that struck Meriwether, Spalding, and Henry Counties

**[Pike, Lamar, Monroe, and Butts Counties](https://www.weather.gov/ffc/2011_tornadoes_5_year_anniv)**

A National Weather Service survey team determined that an EF3 tornado with winds of 140 MPH crossed Pike, Lamar, Monroe and Butts Counties early Thursday morning. The tornado touched down at approximately 1238 AM EDT Thursday morning along highway 19 about 4 miles south of Meansville in south central Pike county. Three houses were destroyed along Piedmont Road about three miles west of Barnesville. Two fatalities occurred when a house was destroyed along Grove Street in Lamar county. A Chevron gas station and a church were destroyed in Barnesville. Three tractor trailers were blown off the road near I-75 at approximately 102 AM EDT. Three houses were damaged, one of which was destroyed. Three people were injured in the damaged house. The tornado lifted in southeast Butts county at approximately 115 AM EDT. The tornado had a path length of approximately 30 miles and a maximum width of six tenths of a mile.

[![Image 5: [ Path of EF-3 tornado that struck Pike, Lamar, Monroe, and Butts counties ]](https://www.weather.gov/images/ffc/events/20110427/pike_tor_track_28april2011_sm.png)](https://www.weather.gov/images/ffc/events/20110427/pike_tor_track_28april2011.png)

 Path of EF-3 tornado that struck Pike, Lamar, Monroe, and Butts Counties

[![Image 6: [ 3-D View of Storm Relative Velocity of the tornado as it tracked across Barnesville. ]](https://www.weather.gov/images/ffc/events/20110427/Barnesville_Tornado_srm.gif)](https://www.weather.gov/images/ffc/events/20110427/Barnesville_Tornado_srm.gif)

 3-D View of the Storm Relative Velocity of the tornado as it tracked across Barnesville. 

 (Courtesy of Jonathan Fox)

**EF2 Tornadoes**

**[Polk, Floyd, and Bartow Counties](https://www.weather.gov/ffc/2011_tornadoes_5_year_anniv)**

A National Weather Service survey team determined that an EF2 tornado with maximum winds of 125 MPH moved across extreme northwest Polk, south Floyd, and Bartow Counties Wednesday evening. The tornado touched down about 6 miles southwest of Cave Springs in Polk county around 845 PM EDT Wednesday. It lifted about 4 miles southwest of Kingston in Bartow county around 925 PM EDT. The path length was 26 miles long and had a width of a half mile wide. More than 13 structures were destroyed and in addition about 10 chicken houses were destroyed.

[![Image 7: [ Path of EF-2 tornado that struck Polk, Floyd, and Bartow Counties. ]](https://www.weather.gov/images/ffc/events/20110427/polk_floyd_bartow_2011april27_sm.png)](https://www.weather.gov/images/ffc/events/20110427/polk_floyd_bartow_2011april27.png)

 Path of EF-2 tornado that struck Polk, Floyd, and Bartow Counties

**[Lumpkin and White Counties](https://www.weather.gov/ffc/2011_tornadoes_5_year_anniv)**

A National Weather Service survey team in conjunction with the White county Emergency Management Staff determined that an EF2 tornado with maximum winds of 120 MPH moved across northeast Lumpkin and into northern White county. The tornado touched down about 5 miles east southeast of Suches in Lumpkin county around 1030 PM EDT Wednesday and tracked 17.5 miles northeast to the White-Habersham county line about 7 miles north northeast of Helen around 1050 PM EDT. This tornado continued into Habersham and Rabun counties where it produced further damage (see the [latest report](https://www.erh.noaa.gov/gsp/localdat/cases/2011/27April_EpicOutbreak/EpicOutbreak.html) from the Greenville-Spartanburg NWS Office for more information). This long tracked tornado downed tens of thousands of trees across the steep terrain of the Chattachoochee National Forest. Due to the remote nature of the area, only 12 homes were damaged, mostly due to trees falling on them. A White county patrolman was trapped on Richard B. Russell Parkway for a few hours after falling trees blocked the road on both sides. The maximum path width was a quarter of a mile. Please note that these photos provide undeniable evidence that mountains and valleys **do not offer any** protection from tornadoes.

[![Image 8: [ Path of EF-2 tornado that struck Lumpkin and White Counties. ]](https://www.weather.gov/images/ffc/events/20110427/LumpkinWhiteEF2TornadoPath_sm.jpg)](https://www.weather.gov/images/ffc/events/20110427/LumpkinWhiteEF2TornadoPath.jpg)

 Path of EF-2 tornado that struck Lumpkin and White Counties

**[Troup county (south of LaGrange)](https://www.weather.gov/ffc/2011_tornadoes_5_year_anniv)**

A National Weather Service survey team determined that an EF2 tornado with winds of 120 MPH developed 5 miles south of LaGrange around 1120 PM EDT Wednesday night. The tornado tracked for 7 miles before lifting around 6 miles east southeast of LaGrange at 1130 PM EDT. The path length was 7 miles and the width was up to one quarter mile. Around 15 homes were destroyed and around 50 homes sustained heavy to minor damage along its path. Thousands of trees were snapped and uprooted with many powerlines down. The most significant damage occurred near Highway 219 and Murphy Road about 2 miles south of the city limits of LaGrange. About 12 homes were destroyed in this area. One home was picked up and thrown 50 feet and its sunroom was thrown 300 yards. A well built log cabin on a hill top was blown off its foundation in the opposite direction of the tornado's movement and destroyed. There were at least 5 injuries in this area as well.

[![Image 9: [ Path of EF-2 tornado that struck Troup county. ]](https://www.weather.gov/images/ffc/events/20110427/TroupEF2TornadoPath_sm.jpg)](https://www.weather.gov/images/ffc/events/20110427/TroupEF2TornadoPath.jpg)

 Path of EF-2 tornado that struck Troup County

**[Harris, Meriwether, and Upson Counties](https://www.weather.gov/ffc/2011_tornadoes_5_year_anniv)**

A National Weather Service survey team determined that an EF2 tornado with winds of 130 MPH crossed Harris, Meriwether, and Upson Counties Wednesday night. The tornado touched down 2 miles northwest of Pine Mountain Valley around 1150 PM EDT Wednesday night and lifted about 9 miles northwest of Thomaston along Highway 74 around 1225 AM EDT. The path length was 24 miles long with an average width of half a mile. Its widest point was close to three quarters of a mile along Highway 354 (just north of Pine Mountain Valley). Thousands of trees were snapped and uprooted with many power lines down. While significant damage was experienced along most of the path with house damage and barns destroyed, the most extensive was located within Franklin Delano State Park. Within the park, it is estimated that 30 percent of the 40 structures located in a campground were heavily damaged or destroyed including a large assembly shelter. Due to the extensive tree damage limiting access within the park, assessments for the precise number of homes and cabins affected are ongoing.

[![Image 10: [ Path of EF-2 tornado that struck Harris, Meriweather, and Upson Counties. ]](https://www.weather.gov/images/ffc/events/20110427/harris_tor_path_2011apr27.JPG)](https://www.weather.gov/images/ffc/events/20110427/harris_tor_path_2011apr27.jpg)

 Path of EF-2 tornado that struck Harris, Meriwether, and Upson Counties

**EF1 Tornadoes**

**[Dade county](https://www.weather.gov/ffc/2011_tornadoes_5_year_anniv) (occurring Wednesday morning)**

A National Weather Service survey team determined that an EF1 tornado with 110 MPH winds tracked from Trenton northward to the Tennessee state line in Dade County at approximately 8:40 AM. The tornado had a path length of 7 miles and was 50 yards wide. There was minor damage to homes and an elementary school.

[![Image 11: [ Path of EF-1 tornado that struck Dade county. ]](https://www.weather.gov/images/ffc/events/20110427/trenton_ef1_tor_track_2011april27_sm.png)](https://www.weather.gov/images/ffc/events/20110427/trenton_ef1_tor_track_2011april27.png)

 Path of EF-1 tornado that struck Dade County at 8:40 AM

**[Dade County](https://www.weather.gov/ffc/2011_tornadoes_5_year_anniv) (occurring Wednesday evening)**

A National Weather Service survey team determined that an EF1 tornado with 110 MPH winds tracked from Fox Mountain to Rising Fawn in Dade County at approximately 7:50 PM. This tornado tracked into the state from Alabama and within Georgia it had a path length of 3 miles and was 100 yards wide.

[![Image 12: [ Path of EF-1 tornado that struck Dade county. ]](https://www.weather.gov/images/ffc/events/20110427/dade_rising_fawn_tor_track_2011april27_sm.png)](https://www.weather.gov/images/ffc/events/20110427/dade_rising_fawn_tor_track_2011april27.png)

 Path of EF-1 tornado that struck Dade County at 7:50 PM

**[Troup, Heard and Coweta Counties](https://www.weather.gov/ffc/2011_tornadoes_5_year_anniv)**

A National Weather Service survey team determined that an EF1 tornado with winds of 90 MPH crossed parts of northeast Troup, southeast Heard and southwest Coweta Counties. The tornado touched down 3 miles west of Hillcrest around 1045 PM EDT Wednesday night and lifted 5 miles northwest of Grantville around 1110 PM EDT Wednesday night. The path length was 17 miles with a maximum width around 100 yards. A hauling trailer and horse trailer were thrown around 20 feet. About 5 homes were damaged in southeast Heard county in and near Miller Road. One home was heavily damaged as it lost two exterior walls and part of its roof. Around 1000 trees were estimated to be snapped or uprooted along its path. No injuries were reported.

[![Image 13: [ Path of EF-1 tornado that struck Troup, Heard, and Coweta counties ]](https://www.weather.gov/images/ffc/events/20110427/TroupHeardCowetaEF1TornadoPath_sm.jpg)](https://www.weather.gov/images/ffc/events/20110427/TroupHeardCowetaEF1TornadoPath.jpg)

 Path of EF-1 tornado that struck Troup, Heard, and Coweta Counties

**[Newton, Morgan, and Greene Counties](https://www.weather.gov/ffc/2011_tornadoes_5_year_anniv)**

A National Weather Service survey team determined that an EF1 tornado with winds of 105 MPH occurred early Thursday morning. It touched down 1 mile west of Newborn in Newton County at approximately 111 AM EDT Thursday morning and lifted 6 miles west of Greensboro in Greene County at approximately 138 AM EDT. It had a path length of 25 miles and a width of half a mile. A shopping center in Madison had a tin roof peeled back. Thousands of trees were downed. Approximately 50 structures sustained damage from downed trees. One trailer had part of the back ripped off. Two trailers sustained tree damage. Three other trailers that were not tied down were flipped.

[![Image 14: [ Path of EF-1 tornado that struck Newton, Morgan, and Greene Counties. ]](https://www.weather.gov/images/ffc/events/20110427/morgan_tor_track_2011april27_sm.jpg)](https://www.weather.gov/images/ffc/events/20110427/morgan_tor_track_2011april27.jpg)

 Path of EF-1 tornado that struck Newton, Morgan, and Greene Counties

**[Putnam and Hancock Counties](https://www.weather.gov/ffc/2011_tornadoes_5_year_anniv)**

A National Weather Service survey team determined that an EF1 tornado with winds of 90 MPH crossed parts of Putnam and Hancock Counties. The tornado touched down 8 miles southeast of Eatonton near Flat Rock around 230 AM EDT Thursday morning, then lifted 8 miles west northwest of Devereux around 305 AM EDT. The path length was 7 miles and the width was around 200 yards. The roof of an outbuilding was lifted off and 4 homes were heavily damaged or destroyed by falling trees. Numerous trees were snapped or uprooted along its path with several powerlines down.

[![Image 15: [ Path of EF-1 tornado that struck Putnam and Hancock Counties. ]](https://www.weather.gov/images/ffc/events/20110427/putnam_hancock_tor_track_2011april28_sm.png)](https://www.weather.gov/images/ffc/events/20110427/putnam_hancock_tor_track_2011april28.png)

 Path of EF-1 tornado that struck Putnam and Hancock Counties

**[Warren County](https://www.weather.gov/ffc/2011_tornadoes_5_year_anniv)**

A National Weather Service survey team determined that an EF1 tornado with winds of 105 MPH touched down 4 miles southwest of Norwood at approximately 339 AM EDT Thursday morning and lifted 1 mile northeast of Camak in Warren County at approximately 351 AM EDT. It had a path length of 8 miles and a width of a quarter of a mile. Eight structures were damaged due to fallen trees and hundreds of trees were downed.

[![Image 16: [ Path of EF-1 tornado that struck Warren county. ]](https://www.weather.gov/images/ffc/events/20110427/warren_tor_track_2011april28_sm.png)](https://www.weather.gov/images/ffc/events/20110427/warren_tor_track_2011april28.png)

 Path of EF-1 tornado that struck Warren County

10.title: Winds of Fury: Mapping the 2011 Tornado Super Outbreak
10.description: In just three days, 367  tornadoes carved a path of destruction across the U.S., leaving 324 people dead and countless lives changed forever
10.content:
In just three days, 367 tornadoes carved a path of destruction across the U.S., leaving 324 people dead and countless lives changed forever

1.   [Introduction](https://storymaps.arcgis.com/stories/9f31004e68dc43ebad657888fae4fcb0#n-NpQ9F7)
2.   [Mapping The Warnings](https://storymaps.arcgis.com/stories/9f31004e68dc43ebad657888fae4fcb0#n-PuoEET)
3.   [The Outbreak](https://storymaps.arcgis.com/stories/9f31004e68dc43ebad657888fae4fcb0#n-0rHPgH)
4.   [Remembering a Tragedy](https://storymaps.arcgis.com/stories/9f31004e68dc43ebad657888fae4fcb0#n-lWivs0)
5.   [References](https://storymaps.arcgis.com/stories/9f31004e68dc43ebad657888fae4fcb0#n-WFndgl)

_Introduction_
--------------

Apr 26-28 2011 Tornado Tracks

The 2011 Super Outbreak was one of the largest, costliest, and deadliest tornado outbreaks in recorded history. It occurred between April 25 and 28, 2011, devastating parts of the Southern, Midwestern, and Northeastern United States. Alabama, Mississippi, and Tennessee were the hardest-hit states, with over 175 tornadoes touching down across their landscapes. Other destructive tornadoes struck Arkansas, Georgia, Kentucky, Louisiana, New York, Virginia, and additional states in the Southern and Eastern U.S., as well as parts of southern Canada.

In total, NOAA's National Weather Service (NWS) and Environment Canada confirmed 367 tornadoes across 21 states, from Texas to New York, and into Canada. Tornado activity was widespread and catastrophic each day, with April 27 marking the peak of destruction. That day alone saw a record-breaking 223 tornadoes touch down within a 24-hour period (midnight to midnight CDT). Among these were four EF5 tornadoes, the most intense classification on the Enhanced Fujita scale, which are typically rare and occur only about once per year.

This outbreak left a trail of catastrophic destruction, forever altering communities in its path.

### _The Formation of the Storms_

Weather Prediction Center Surface Analysis valid at 1:00 PM CT 4/27/11. Note the upper level trough around the low pressure (L) systems.

The outbreak was triggered by a vigorous upper-level trough that moved into the Southern Plains on April 25. Ahead of this trough, an extratropical cyclone formed between northeastern Oklahoma and western Missouri, gradually moving northeast. Similar atmospheric conditions persisted on April 26, with forecasts indicating a high likelihood of severe thunderstorms, including strong to violent long-track tornadoes during the afternoon and evening.

By April 27, as the system progressed eastward toward the Ohio, Mississippi, and Tennessee Valleys, a powerful mid-level jet stream of 80–100 knots accompanied the trough. This jet stream generated strong wind shear, while a low-pressure center quickly moved northeastward across the region. During the afternoon, CAPE values between 2000 and 3000 J/kg were observed across Louisiana and southern Mississippi, with moderate instability spreading into the southern Tennessee Valley. Temperatures in the southeastern U.S. ranged from the mid-70s °F (mid-20s °C) to the lower 90s °F (near 35 °C), and helicity values of 450–600 m²/s² supported the development of significant tornadic activity, including strong and long-track tornadoes.

_Mapping The Warnings_
----------------------

A large area of possible severe storms for April 25–27 was forecasted as the Storm Prediction Center(SPC) issued a moderate risk of severe weather for three consecutive days, centered over Arkansas through Tennessee. At 3:25 p.m.CDT April 25, 2011, the SPC issued a particularly dangerous situation(PDS)tornado watch for much of Arkansas and parts of Missouri, Oklahoma, Texas, and Louisiana.

A high risk of severe weather was issued for April 26 for portions of Louisiana, Arkansas, Oklahoma, and Texas along and near the Interstate 30 corridor as conditions became even more favorable for extreme weather. A large PDS tornado watch with very high possibilities for tornadoes was issued for that same area that afternoon. Widespread tornado warnings were then issued in that area later that evening

Significant severe weather was ongoing early on April 27 (in the overnight hours) and continued the whole day. For the second day in a row, the SPC issued a high risk of severe weather for the Southern United States. Later that morning, the SPC even increased the probability for tornadoes to 45 percent along a corridor from Meridian, Mississippi, to[Huntsville, Alabama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Huntsville,_Alabama), an extremely rare issuance exceeding the high risk standards. Conditions became increasingly favorable for tornadoes during such an extreme tornado outbreak.

Storm Prediction Center Convective Outlooks (day3, day2, day1) valid from 12pm April 27 until 12pmApril 28, 2011. Images are in chronological order from left to right.

### _Convective Outlooks_

The Storm Prediction Center (SPC) is part of the National Weather Service (NWS) and the National Centers for Environmental Prediction (NCEP). Their mission is to provide timely and accurate forecasts and watches for severe weather over the contiguous United States.

The Storm Prediction Center (SPC) issues Day 1, Day 2, and Day 3 Convective Outlooks to identify areas of non-severe and severe thunderstorm potential across the contiguous United States. These outlooks include both graphical forecasts and a detailed text narrative. The categorical forecast conveys the overall level of severe weather threat using a numerical scale (e.g., 5), descriptive terms (e.g., HIGH), and corresponding colors (e.g., magenta). The probabilistic forecast provides an estimated likelihood of a severe weather event occurring within 25 miles of a specific point.

SPC Convective Outlook day 1 valid from 1pm April 27 until 12pmApril 28, 2011. Images are in chronological order from top-left to bottom right. (categorial, tornado, wind, hail).

The text narrative begins with a list of severe thunderstorm risk areas, organized by state or geographic region, followed by a clear and concise summary of the expected threats (e.g., tornadoes, damaging winds, hail) and their timing, with a focus on the highest-risk areas. This discussion typically begins with a synopsis section that outlines the broader weather pattern and highlights key features influencing thunderstorm development. Additional sections of the discussion are divided by geographic regions, where the text provides detailed meteorological analysis to explain the reasoning behind the forecasted storm coverage, intensity, and type of severe weather threats.

### _Watches and Warnings_

If development of severe thunderstorms is imminent, or likely to occur in the next several hours, the next step is a**Severe Thunderstorm**or**Tornado Watch**. Such watches alert the public, aviators and local NWS offices that environmental conditions have become favorable for the development of severe storms or tornadoes. Local storm spotter networks activate; and forecasters in the threat area closely monitor radar imagery and spotter reports to issue the appropriate severe thunderstorm and tornado warnings. **A watch is not a warning**, and should not be interpreted as a guarantee that there will be severe weather!

Whenever there is a high confidence forecast of multiple intense tornadoes (rated EF2-EF5), SPC will highlight a watch with the following**"PDS"**wording:

> **_...THIS IS A PARTICULARLY DANGEROUS SITUATION..._**

When severe hail (at least 1-inch diameter), damaging winds (at least 50 knots or 58 mph) or a tornado appear imminent, local NWS offices will issue a**Severe Thunderstorm Warning**or**Tornado Warning**as appropriate. The warning rapidly disseminated over NOAA Weather radio and various mass and social media channels, so that people in the warning area can find safe shelter to take cover from the storm.

### _Mesoscale Discussions_

The Storm Prediction Center (SPC) issues Mesoscale Discussions (MDs or MCDs) to highlight the potential for severe thunderstorms over the continental U.S. within the next six hours, with a primary focus on the first 1-3 hours. These discussions address three main scenarios:

1.   The development or evolution of severe storms in relation to ongoing or potential weather watches.
2.   Notifying users of an expected categorical upgrade in the Day 1 Convective Outlook.
3.   Categorical upgrades to the 0100 UTC Day 1 Convective Outlook following the issuance of the 0600 UTC outlook.

different types of mesoscale discussions all uploaded by the SPC on April 27, 2011. Click an image to read the full MD discussion

A full example of a Mesoscale discussion uploaded by the SPC

Each MD includes a reference to ongoing watches (e.g., _TORNADO WATCH 559_) or an assessment of the likelihood of a watch being issued, along with the expected type of watch. Confidence levels are communicated using phrases such as:

*   **SEVERE POTENTIAL...WATCH UNLIKELY** (5% or 20%)
*   **SEVERE POTENTIAL...WATCH POSSIBLE** (40% or 60%)
*   **SEVERE POTENTIAL...WATCH LIKELY** (80% or 95%)
*   **SEVERE POTENTIAL...TORNADO WATCH LIKELY** (80% or 95%)
*   **SEVERE POTENTIAL...SEVERE THUNDERSTORM WATCH LIKELY** (80% or 95%)
*   **SEVERE POTENTIAL...WATCH NEEDED SOON** (95%)

Each MD begins with a plain-language summary detailing the forecasted severe weather threat, including timing, coverage, intensity, and storm mode, as well as the SPC's planned actions. The second paragraph provides a more technical explanation, focusing on mesoscale features and atmospheric processes expected to drive storm development.

Severe weather MDs are issued when mesoscale insights can provide valuable information about convective developments. Written concisely and in accessible language, these discussions emphasize mesoscale details to help users prepare ahead of severe weather watches. The SPC strives to issue MDs concerning severe potential 1-2 hours before a watch is officially released, offering advanced lead time for operational readiness.

_The Outbreak_
--------------

Chart ranking confirmed tornados during the outbreak. Credit: Wikipedia

### April 25, 2011

People walk on a road in Vilonia, Ark., Tuesday, April 26, 2011, after a tornado hit the area late Monday. The storm system killed at least seven people, including three who drowned in floods in northwest Arkansas. (AP Photo/Danny Johnston)

The first day of the outbreak had been anticipated a few days before from the warnings. But no one was aware of how bad the next few days were about to be.

By the evening hours of April 25, tornadoes had been reported across a few states, some of which caused significant damage in Arkansas. An intense supercell thunderstorm tracked near the Little Rock area and a tornado emergency was declared for the city of Vilonia. A large EF2 wedge tornado struck the town, subsequently causing severe damage and killing four people. A strong EF3 tornado had also struck the Hot Springs Village area earlier that evening; that tornado caused severe damage and resulted in one death. Later that evening, another EF2 tornado caused extensive damage to both a school building and Little Rock Air Force Base as well. Severe flooding continued across a large area from the Red River valley to the Great Lakes.

A total of 42 tornadoes and five tornado-related deaths were confirmed on the 25th.

### April 26, 2011

_Numerous Trees snpped and uprooted near Dubberly LA along HWY 531. Credit: NWS_ Shreveport, LA

Tornado watches were issued for the Lower Great Lakes during the afternoon hours as supercell thunderstorms developed along the warm front lifting north across central Michigan. Two tornadoes touched down in Michigan and caused damage to farm structures. Further east, severe thunderstorms caused scattered wind damage and large hail across Pennsylvania and New York. Two-inch-diameter hail was reported in Lock Haven, Pennsylvania.An isolated supercell moved across Central New York throughout much of the afternoon, producing golf ball-sized hail in Syracuse and spawning two tornados that caused damage.

_Radar image taken from 7:13 PM showing the 4 supercells in East TX and Northwest LA. Credit: NWS_ Shreveport, LA

The second surface low corresponded to an area of strong upper level divergence ahead of the downstream shortwave. As the low formed across Texas and deepened while moving east, a tightening pressure gradient force further strengthened the low-level jet, therefore creating a broad warm sector across the southeastern states. This also generated stronger wind shear, providing better organization for the supercell storms as a result. Numerous tornadoes touched down across several states, including Texas, Louisiana, and Arkansas. Most of those tornadoes were weak, but a few of them caused considerable damage. A long-tracked wedge tornado caused EF2 damage in rural portions of Texas and Louisiana. An EF3 tornado destroyed structures and caused severe damage at Fort Campbell, Kentucky, as well.

A total of 55 tornadoes were confirmed on the 26th, although no fatalities occurred.

### April 27, 2011

April 27, 2011 tornado survivor recalls that life-altering day

Today was arguably the most intense and damaging day of the outbreak.

The Storm Prediction Center received 292 reports of tornadoes in the preceding 24 hours.In addition to setting the record for most tornadoes in a calendar day (223; midnight to midnight CDT (05:00 – 05:00 UTC)), it also broke the record for the most tornado touchdowns in any 24-hour period with 226 from 12:40 a.m. to 12:40 a.m. CDT (05:40 – 05:40 UTC) April 27–28, breaking the old 24-hour record of 148 set by the 1974 Super Outbreak. Of those 226 tornadoes, 59 touched down in Alabama and 83 began in Tennessee, accounting for 62.8 percent of the tornadoes that touched down on April 27.

On April 27 alone, the National Weather Service in Huntsville, Alabama, issued 92 tornado warnings, 31 severe thunderstorm warnings, and seven flash flood warnings. a total of 238 tornado-related deaths would be confirmed in the state Alabama alone, with a total of 316 deaths in the country.

#### The morning outbreak

The Cullman Tornado, as seen from near Guntersville, Alabama. Picture courtesy of WAFF-TV

A majority of the tornadoes embedded in this initial squall line were weak, though several were strong and as such caused significant damage. An EF3 tornado caused major damage to homes in Coaling, Alabama, an EF2 and an EF3 tornado produced severe damage and a fatality near Eupora, Mississippi. Another EF3 tornado resulted in heavy damage in downtown Cordova, Alabama, which was struck by a violent EF4 tornado later that afternoon. An EF2 also struck Cahaba Heights near Birmingham. One embedded cell began producing tornadoes just after 5:00 a.m. CDT (10:00 UTC), starting with an EF1 tornado striking Berry, Alabama. This was soon followed by the Cordova EF3 tornado. As the line entered Cullman County, Alabama, the cell, a mesoscale convective vortex(MCV), began exhibiting a comma head appearance and produced another long-tracked EF2 tornado that struck the town of[Hanceville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hanceville,_Alabama), killing one person. The MCV would then produce 13 tornadoes (most rated EF1) to the northeast in Marshall County, many of which occurred simultaneously. Two more tornadoes were produced as the comma head-shaped embedded cell continued northeast along the Jackson/DeKalb county line, including a long-track EF1 that resulted in a fatality near Pisgah. The same area was impacted later that day by a high-end EF4 tornado. Another EF1 tornado occurred in Dade County, Georgia, with the cell, and six more tornadoes struck Hamilton County, Tennessee, five of which were in the Chattanooga area. The 26th and final tornado produced by the MCV was an EF2 tornado in northern Bradley County, Tennessee, which hit at 9:45 a.m. EDT (13:45 UTC).

The initial storms caused widespread power and telephone line outages across Alabama and Tennessee. This line of storms also caused some NOAA weather radio transmitter sites to stop functioning for the remainder of the outbreak. Because of this, more than one million customers were without power and had no warning of any approaching tornadoes later that day.

Interactive map of the _Tuscaloosa-Birmingham EF-4 Tornado track April 27, 2011. Credit: NWS KBMX_

#### The afternoon storms

The most intense supercells of the outbreak developed around midday in central Mississippi and began tracking eastward. With the extreme instability and wind shear, they quickly intensified and eventually became tornadic, shortly thereafter resulting in strong to violent tornadoes. Responding to the high risk issued by the SPC and the already unstable atmosphere expected to become even more unstable throughout the afternoon hours, a[PDS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Particularly_dangerous_situation)[tornado watch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_watch)was issued at 1:45 p.m. CDT (18:45 UTC) for much of Alabama and portions of Mississippi, Tennessee, and Georgia. A widespread complex of supercell storms overspread the states of Mississippi and Alabama and violent tornadoes began rapidly touching down as the afternoon progressed.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak#cite_note-April_27_Conditions_HUN-41)

By mid-afternoon, as wind shear and low-level moisture continued to dramatically increase, a tornado emergency was declared for Neshoba County, Mississippi, as a large tornado was reported on the ground by both storm spotters and a camera atop a television tower from ABC affiliate WTOK-TV(channel 11) in Meridian, Mississippi. This powerful EF5 tornado caused incredible damage northeast of Philadelphia, Mississippi, where pavement was torn off from roads, vehicles were thrown, and the ground was scoured out to a depth of 2 feet (0.61 m) by the tornado. Three people died when a mobile home was thrown 300 yards (270 m) into a wooded area, obliterating it in the process. Another very long-tracked EF4 tornado passed near the town of Enterprise, Mississippi, killing seven people before crossing into Alabama and eventually dissipating. Four tornadoes were officially rated EF5 on the Enhanced Fujita scale that day. One of those EF5 tornadoes struck the town of Smithville, Mississippi, where many well-built brick homes were reduced to bare slabs, numerous hardwood trees were completely debarked, and an SUV was hurled half a mile into the top of the town's water tower, subsequently leaving behind a visible dent. Another long-tracked EF5 wedge tornado passed through rural portions of Alabama and Tennessee, becoming the deadliest tornado of the outbreak as it completely devastated the towns of[Hackleburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hackleburg,_Alabama),Phil Campbell,Mount Hope,Tanner, and Harvest, killing 72 people. This marks only the second day in history (after April 3, 1974) that there were more than two F5/EF5 tornadoes reported.

image of the 0.5 degree reflectivity data from KBMX at 538 pm of the circulation as it crossed over the Tuscaloosa-Jefferson County line. Credit: NWS KBMX

The tornadoes continued tracking through central Alabama that afternoon and into the early evening hours. A dangerous and destructive tornado struck the city of Cullman, Alabama, at around 3:00 p.m. CDT (20:00 UTC). This large, multiple-vortex tornado was captured on several tower cameras from television stations out of Birmingham. The tornado caused extensive destruction in the city's downtown area; it was ultimately rated EF4. The final damage count was 867 residences and 94 businesses in Cullman; six people died as well. The town of Cordova, Alabama, which had already been damaged by an EF3 tornado from the initial round of storms, was struck by an EF4 tornado that killed 13 people. Two violent EF4 tornadoes also ripped through Jackson County, Alabama, one of which caused a fatality near Bridgeport while the other passed near[Pisgah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pisgah,_Alabama)and into Georgia where it caused major damage in Trenton and killed 14 people.

Aerial View of Scope of Damage Path. Credit: NWS KBMX

At around 5:10 p.m. CDT (22:10 UTC), a very large and exceptionally destructive tornado struck Tuscaloosa, Alabama, and about 40 minutes later, that same tornado struck the northern suburbs of nearby Birmingham.A tornado emergency was issued for both cities, along with many other cities that day. Many local television stations broadcast live footage of this long-tracked tornado in both Tuscaloosa and Birmingham. A debris ball was observed by the Birmingham[NEXRAD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NEXRAD), indicating that the tornado was causing extreme damage.This tornado killed 64 people and caused extensive devastation in densely populated areas. The supercell that produced the Tuscaloosa/Birmingham EF4 tornado originated in Newton County, Mississippi. The same supercell produced another EF4 tornado later that evening that killed 22 people and struck the Ohatchee, Alabama, area and eventually crossed into Georgia, causing additional damage near Cave Spring before dissipating. Further to the south, a mile-wide EF3 tornado killed 7 people in mostly rural areas and caused major damage in the small town of Eoline. The final EF5 tornado of the day caused remarkable damage in and around the town of Rainsville, Alabama, killing 25 people before crossing into Georgia and dissipating.

Homes and businesses lie in ruins along 15th St. in Tuscaloosa, Ala. Wednesday, April 27, 2011. Credit: Dusty Compton / Tuscaloosa News

Tornadoes continued touching down further to the northeast as the sun set, particularly in Georgia. This included a long-tracked EF4 tornado that caused major damage in Ringgold, Georgia,Apison, Tennessee, and Cleveland, Tennessee, killing 20 people along the path. After dark, violent tornadoes continued to touch down, and a nighttime EF4 tornado destroyed many lakeside homes at Lake Martin in eastern Alabama, killing seven people. Additional strong nighttime tornadoes occurred in Georgia, including an EF3 that killed two people in Barnesville, and another EF3 that destroyed homes and killed one person at Lake Burton.

#### Into the Evening

Downed trees resulting from an EF4 tornado that tracked through the park on April 27, 2011. Credit: NPS

Powerful tornadoes touched down across Tennessee as well that evening. A violent EF4 struck the community of New Harmony, Tennessee, where homes were leveled, vehicles were tossed, and four people were killed.Two EF3 tornadoes crossed paths in Greene and Washington counties (coming a couple hours apart), resulting in eight fatalities. The rural communities of Horse Creek and Camp Creek suffered major damage from those tornadoes late that evening. A very large EF4 wedge tornado leveled a mile-wide swath of forest through 14 miles (23 km) of Great Smoky Mountains National Park, resulting in many trails being closed.At Chilhowee Lake, large metal power line truss towers were torn and thrown from their concrete supports that they were anchored to.

A secondary area of severe weather also developed that afternoon and evening along a corridor extending from central and northern Virginia northward through Maryland,Pennsylvania, and New York, continuing into early April 28. Many tornadoes touched down in this area as well. Most of these tornadoes were weak, though an EF2 tornado touched down near the town of Halifax, Virginia, and caused severe damage to homes in the area, resulting in one death.Tornado alerts were issued for Southern Ontario as far north as Ottawa as well; one tornado was later confirmed in Fergus, Ontario.

### April 28, 2011

Tornado watches were issued for the Atlantic coast from Pennsylvania to Florida at the start of the day and continued through the morning and early afternoon, but tornadoes were forecasted to generally be weaker and more isolated. Despite this, the secondary portion of the outbreak that had begun producing scattered tornadoes throughout the Mid-Atlantic and East Coast regions the previous evening intensified during the early hours of the morning, producing numerous tornadoes. A particularly active region, in which there were some strong tornadoes, was the Interstate 81 corridor extending from southwest Virginia, northward through the Shenandoah Valley and into Pennsylvania, and New York. This included the deadly EF3 tornado that struck the town of Glade Spring, Virginia, very early in the morning, where three people died.Tornadoes were also reported in Florida,Georgia,South Carolina,North Carolina,and Maryland. Most of these tornadoes were weak.

In the wake of the tornadoes and severe thunderstorms, widespread flooding hit the Midwest, South, and Eastern Seaboard, with extensive flood and flash flood warnings issued.The last tornadoes of the outbreak touched down that afternoon in eastern North Carolina, though the tornadoes that impacted the area this time around were weak. The system moved out into the Atlantic Ocean that evening, with the exception of isolated thunderstorms over central Florida that night into April 29, although no more tornadoes were produced.

01 / 05

The Rainsville tornado exiting town at EF5 strength.

Formed: April 27, 2011, 6:19 p.m Dissipated: April 27, 2011, 6:55 p.m. Duration: 36 minutes

Highest winds: >200 mph (320 km/h) Overall effects: 25 fatalities, unknown injuries

The tornado in Philadelphia MS

Formed: April 27, 2011, 2:30 p.m. Dissipated: April 27, 2011, 3:00 p.m. Duration: 30 minutes

Highest winds: 205 mph (330 km/h) Overall effects: 3 fatalities, 8 injuries

The tornado in downtown Cullman AL

Formed: April 27, 2011, 2:40 p.m. Dissipated: April 27, 2011, 3:38 p.m. Duration: 58 minutes

Highest winds: 190 mph (310 km/h) Overall effects: 6 fatalities, 48+ injuries

The tornado as it moved through Tuscaloosa at EF4 intensity.

Formed: April 27, 2011, 4:43 p.m. Dissipated: April 27, 2011, 6:14 p.m. Duration: 1 hour, 31 minutes

Highest winds:190 mph (310 km/h) Overall effects: 64 fatalities, ~1,500 injuries

The Shoal Creek Valley/Ohatchee EF4 tornado.

Formed: April 27, 2011, 6:28 p.m. Dissipated: April 27, 2011, 9:15 p.m. Duration: 1 hour, 47 minutes

Highest winds: 180 mph (290 km/h) Overall effects: 22 fatalities, 85 injuries

Remembering a Tragedy
---------------------

I myself have been facisinated with severe weather since I was a child. I was only 7 years old when this happened, but I remember seeing it on the news. When I first started studying meteorology, this was one of the first weather events I looked into. Every time I come back to this event, it breaks my heart. What a tragic day. My heart goes out to everyone that lost their life, to their families, to the people who lost everything. We cant stop tornados from happening, but we can research them and forecast them and do our best to prevent such horrible tragedies like the 2011 super outbreak.

I hope that you not only learned something today, but also were touched and moved like I was just reading about the events of the outbreak.

Thank-you.

In Memoriam- April 27, 2011
